p: When I talked about recurring training for officers, it’s not just police officers–
[interposing] Okay.
it’s also sergeants and lieutenants.
Okay.

And so what that time, that week block will give us is the ability to review with them things just like that. And I believe with things like that you can’t do it haphazardly. It has to be done thoughtfully and systematically, and that weeklong new training initiative I think is the way to make sure that that is done thoughtfully and systematically.

Okay. My second question is about headcount in the sense that, obviously, you’re going to deploy officers based on where the stats and everything else, but particularly in my district there’s always- and this is not just this year. This has been going on for years in the previous administration as well where I’m told there’s not enough officers to do certain things and

all of that. So, I don’t know where to take that to or how that works on a–
[interposing] So, if you have questions about your specific district headcount, I’m happy to work with you on it off line.
Okay. Okay. Thank you very much, Commissioner. That’s it, Chair. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Council Member Schulman. Also, before we move onto the next Council Member, just want to recognize our students from PS21 in the Bronx who have joined us. Thank you for joining us and welcome to the People’s House. Next we’ll hear from Council Member Linda Lee.

Thank you, Chair. Sorry. Sorry I was late. I’m trying to bounce around different hearings for the Prelim Budget. So, I was actually just reading this because I wanted to see if the answers were in there for my questions, but I’ll just go ahead. So, thank you so much, Commissioner, for all the work you do. I have four precincts in my district and they’re all amazing and we work very closely with them. So, thank you so much for all the work that you are doing at the NYPD. And I don’t

know if this was asked about the Chief Savings Officers. I know that every agency has a plan to find out where exactly some of the savings can be found. And just wanted to know who will complete the comprehensive assessment for the agency spending and has been designated as the Chief Savings officer, and what areas of spending are being looked at for savings, and what are the target reductions for FY26 and 27?

So, I’m very happy to introduce you personally to our brand new– newly-minited Chief Savings Officer of the New York CIty Police Department, our Deputy Commissioner of Management and Budget, Kristine Ryan, who spent actually the vast majority of her career at the Office of Management and Budget, and she can very ably answer any question you have on this topic. Go ahead, Kristine.
Okay, great.

Good morning. So, yes, I am the designated Chief Savings Officer. So, the targets that we’ve been given just like the other agencies, it’s 1.5 percent in fiscal year 26 and 2.5 percent going forward. That 1.5 percent is about a

$90 million reduction expectation in the current fiscal year, and $154 in the baseline. On top of that, the expectation is that 50 percent of our civilian vacancies will be reduced and the value of that is $46 million each year. So combined, the target is 137 million in the current year, and 200 million next year, and a little hire beyond that. So, we’re looking at the entire agency's budget. We really have to balance, obviously, what our operational needs are with where we can find savings, and I think one of the critical things to emphasize here are what– are the things we’ve already done. As the Commissioner mentioned earlier, we have seen reductions in overtime which is a significant part of our budget, reducing calendar year over calendar year $143 million which was 12.4 percent of our overtime budget, and for the first half of this fiscal year, we’ve seen a reduction of $88 million over that same period last year which is 14.1 percent reduction. So, we do this all the time. It’s not specific to this specific target that was given for this Executive Budget or specific time period. It’s

something that I work on with my team even before I became Chief Savings Officer, to try to make sure we’re utilizing our resources responsibly. It is something that within the scope of our agency, because more than 90 percent of our budget is personnel, it does become something we really need to look at what we can do safely and effectively and balancing the fiscal needs of the city with the operational needs of our Department.

And are there areas that you’ve identified aside from the overtime, you know, regular underspending with– of course, the goal is not to, you know, make sure that– to make sure that the service levels stay the same. But looking at areas, have you identified any areas that are regularly underspent?
So, we’re still doing that review and we’re still having those conversations with City Hall and with OMB, so we’ll have more information on that as we get closer to the Executive Budget.

Okay. In the past, I know that NYPD utilized asset forfeiture to bolster the

budget and what specific expenses can NYPD use asset forfeiture funding for?

So, asset forfeiture has to be utilized for cost and expenditures tied to law enforcement. And that can be anything from investigations. It could be tied to training. It could be tied to education, travel for that training and education and equipment for law enforcement officers and law enforcement operations. And we follow very– follow strictly the federal guidelines on the usage of asset forfeiture.
Okay and have you looked at decreasing or eliminating any units with NYPD as a way to cost save?
Again, all those conversations are still ongoing right now.

Okay. And this is a question that I have been personally more and more interested in terms of the use AI technology. I actually have a colleague and friend that worked in Chicago PD and used– created an entire AI new system and platform for the Police Department in Chicago to help reduce overtime which actually also helped in terms of scheduling and planning of all the different

precincts as well so that they were able to better plan out who was going to work in what shift. And so just wondering if that use of technology has been utilized here for the overtime as well?
We haven’t adopted anything like that yet. Obviously, any use of AI we’d want to do responsibly and thoughtfully.
Yep.
So, I think we’re looking to see what other police departments are doing, but you know, proceeding cautiously as a result.

Okay. I would love to have a separate conversation offline about this, because not just with PD, but I think in general there are ways to utilize it safely, whether you’re talking about health care, you know, having different city agencies communicate better and share data, of course in a safe way, to just figure out how we can understand if we are actually serving New Yorkers effectively, right? So, even in cases like B-HEARD and other, you know, mental health-related non-police response services, that cuts across multiple agencies. So how

do we know if people are actually not falling through the cracks, and that we’re better serving them. So, I’d be curious to have that conversation offline afterwards.
Happy to.

And then just really quickly, my last couple questions are around Domain Awareness System and mobility [sic]. About a decade ago in conjunction with Microsoft, the NYPD developed the Domain Awareness System. So, do sales of the system to other municipalities generate revenue for the city?
Once upon a time they did, but my understanding is that in the past several years those sales have dried up.
Okay. And were there any funding that the city received last year at all, or–
[interposing] I don’t believe so, but Kristine can require– can–
[interposing] In terms of revenue?
Yes.
No.
Okay and does Microsoft retain information collected by the system?
No. We own all the information.
Okay, perfect. Alright, that's it. Thank you, Chair.
Thank you so much. Council Member Lee–
[interposing] But it’s in – sorry, it is in Microsoft cloud, but is our instance of the cloud and we own the data. They do not.
Got it. Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member. Next, we'll hear from Council Member Encarnacion and then Wong and then Brewer. And then Nurse and then Ariola.
Hello, Commissioner, good morning, still morning.
Hello.

I wanted to thank you for specifically addressing immigration in your statement. And also, you know, obviously you saw our Speaker, our Chair, both brought up questions in regards to immigration that is extremely important.

As the Chair of the Immigration, it’s important to me. And I’m happy to hear that the seven recommendations out of the DOI report will be implemented but can you tell maybe a timeline for the roll out specifically around like the policy, the stand alone policy and the trainings that were recommended?
Sure. Our Deputy Commissioner for Legal Matters, Michael Gerber, will answer that question.

Right. So, we’re implementing all the recommendations and that’s going to be done at some point in the second quarter of this year. And we– because we want to do it holistically, right? We want to– we’re not going to do it piece meal, but by the end of the second quarter of this year, we’re going to have sort of revamp the policy, incorporated all of DOI’s recommendations, and then like I said, it’ll be rolled out before the end of the second quarter.

And can you talk a little bit– I know that the report was favorable to what you were in line with, but there was one specific local law that was mentioned, 246, in

regards to you all trying to get compliance with that law. Can you speak a little bit about that and the specifics?

Right. So, there were actually two local laws that were flagged. Both really– so one is a reporting issue. Totally fair point from DOI. It didn’t go to the substance of what we were doing, but how we were reporting our data. So, we’re fixing that. The other issue, I think it’s a fair point, but it’s a little bit technical. So, under city law, we have to have a separate distinct policy about the use of Department facilities by law enforcement agencies other than the NYPD. We had not developed that free-standing policy which we’re in the process of doing. What I want to be clear about and the DOI report makes this clear as well. We already had in our policy, and quite clearly so, that Department facilities like all Department resources cannot be used in connection with civil immigration enforcement, period, full stop. So, it wasn't a substantive issue, but as DOI pointed out, we are required to have a free-standing

policy about the use of facilities in this regard, and we’re developing that.

And I will add, obviously we’re always interested in continual improvement and we will continue to improve in this agency, but I am incredibly proud of the way that the New York City Police Department has handled itself on this issue, certainly in the face of unreasonable pressure not to comply.

Thank you for that. And I know that you spoke also in your testimony about in-service training taking place with all of the officers. Are the sanctuary city’s policies a part of those training? Will they be incorporated in the trainings– [inaudible]

Of course. And the good thing about these trainings is the issue of the day may change year to year or every two years, or for every few years, and so those trainings can be updated to reflect like the current reality.

And in the last 35 seconds, I’m going to try to sneak this in. But you also mentioned 200 additional cops for specialized

units. I wanted to ask specifically about the Narcotics Unit and what the headcount is for that.
About the what unit?
The Narcotics Unit.

Okay. So, I spoke about 200 additional cops in the context of the borough split in the Bronx. Manhattan, Queens, Brooklyn, they are one– each one geographic borough but for the Police Department they’re organized into two different patrol boroughs. The Bronx is on par or exceeds one or all of those boroughs in a number of different categories. We’d look like 911 calls, crime complaints, etcetera, violence. And so I believe that it was long overdue to move the Bronx from a single patrol borough structure to a dual patrol borough structure. So later this year, we’ll be separating the Bronx into Patrol Borough Bronx North and Patrol Borough Bronx South. As part of that, the borough of the Bronx will get 200 additional officers. Many of them will be for specialty units that a patrol borough would get. So, evidence collection teams, homicide squads, narcotics,–
[interposing] But we don’t have the breakdown of numbers there?
Crime analysis, all of that. I’m sorry?
But we don’t have the numbers, the breakdown of numbers of exactly how many–
[interposing] If you want the breakdown of how the 200 will be assigned, we can get that to you after.
Okay, perfect.
Do you have that here? We’ll get it to you after.
We can get it to you after.
Perfect. Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member Encarnacion. Next, we’ll hear from Council Member Wong.

Thank you, Chair. Thank you, Commissioner, for coming today. Public safety is the first thing my constituents expect from the city. In the Middle Village, Maspeth, Glendale, Elmhurst, Regal Park, and Ridgewood, residents tell

me they value the NYPD. They know the officers in the 104th, 110th and 112th precincts by name and they appreciate the work that is being done under difficult conditions. My questions today will focus on whether the 104th, 110 and 112 precincts are properly staffed from patrol to the detective squads and how NYPD and the Transportation Bureau plan to sustain proactively quality of life and Vision Zero enforcements. My first question for each of the 104th, 110 and 112 precincts, can you provide the current authorized and actual uniformed headcounts?
We’ll get that to you after this hearing.

Okay, thank you. Next issue is that we have a lot of car meet-ups in our district in which dozens of cars meet up, whether they make donuts, loud music, you know, and they travel around from district to district. They often start at the Maspeth industrial areas and they go all over the city. I get these calls whether it’s two in the morning or whether it’s four in the morning, and– what is being done to effectively combat these issues?
Our Chief of Department, Chief Mike LiPetri will speak to the plans for addressing car meet-ups.
Morning.
Morning.

So, as tasked to the Chief of Patrol and the borough commanders across the city, not just in Patrol Borough Queens North, we have a substantial car meet plan that is reviewed daily, and before the weekend on Friday, all the information, the intelligence that we are getting is then operationalized for deployment, not just within one precinct, but across the city. We also know specific bridges that some of these car meets will then actually leave the car meet or come into a specific area, notably Queens North. Just last night, I’ll give you an example. Though not a car meet, but a substantial vehicular crime happened in the 109 precinct, and within 15 minutes those individuals were driving to the Bronx. We had intelligence of what bridge they were going over. We had intelligence of where they were going to end up, and they were apprehended and arrested on a vehicular-related crime. The same intelligence and

the same deployment is done for car meets. And just one other thing. The 311 and the 911 data that we get prior to historically is analyzed and again we are deploying to locations that we’ve known in the past have had those types of meetups.

Thank you. My next– do I have time for another question? I used to serve on the School Board, Community Education Council 24, and during the last years of the de Blasio he wanted to dismiss all the school safety agents and replace them with like community patrol, and as a result of that a lot of school safety agents left. And in my recent visits to schools, and I noticed that many of these vacancies have not been filled up. So, is there a policy? Is there something you would to support to hire back for the school safety agents that left before they were totally let go?

We would gladly take them back. I’ll be honest. The title of school safety agent is one that we are having difficulty recruiting for. We have done a lot to reorganize our school safety division, including putting approximately 100 school safety agents who are working administrative jobs like back in schools, but that is an example of

a title where our actual headcount is significantly under our budgeted headcount. And so we are looking at a number of different ways that we can have the same success we had with school safety agents going forward that we recently had in terms of hiring police officers, including working with DCAS to see if the test is testing the right thing, seeing if we can give the test more frequently. Just generally taking a look at how we test for, hire for, and recruit for the position of school safety agent. One area that we’ve had a lot of success in over the past year and we worked very closely with the previous Council on this is creating this assistant school safety agent title. And we have now hired about 114 of them. And that new title will serve as a pathway into the school safety agent title.
Okay. Thank you.
Thank you.
Thank you so much, Council Member Wong. Next, we’ll hear from Council Member Brewer.
Okay. Thank you very much. You’re doing a great job, but expect no less.
Thank you.

So, the 24, the 20, Manhattan North and Central Park are great, great leaders. And thank you for answering all my letters. I write hundreds and you answer them all. And I think– I know you know you think they’re nuts, but I appreciate the answer.
I don’t think they’re nuts.
I appreciate it.
They’re a lot.
I know. Everybody gets a lot. I write 50 letters a week.
I know.

I know you know. Thank you. So, retail theft, domestic violence, and paperwork. So, on the retail theft, in one case I got Duanne Reede [sp?] to put in security and then in other cases they didn’t. And so of course, it’s a challenge in the place that doesn’t have any security. So, I just didn’t know how many resources? Is it an issue? How are we doing it?

Okay, we have a great story to tell on retail theft. Last year, we had significant declines in retail theft. This year, we're seeing even greater declines, and what we’ve

done is we have completely overhauled our approach to addressing retail theft, including but not limited to actually investigating cases of retail theft. We know retail theft tends to be our recidivist crime, and we are now treating it as such, and our Chief of Department, Chief LiPetri who is really let the effort to come up with this new strategy that has had such great results can tell you more about how we're doing it.
And the numbers if you can. Thank you.
Good morning.
Good morning.

So, this year, the City of New York has seen a 20 percent decrease in retail theft on top of the decrease in retail theft last year, and it really goes out to the men and women of the New York City Police Department and the investigators that now are investigating petty theft. Those complaints were never investigated. They were basically closed. Nothing was done with them. We’ve now tasked our detectives to investigate petty theft, and what we see is that the same person that might be stealing less than a thousand dollars at a CVS, which

the complaint report would be closed, is also committing another petty theft in a different CVS maybe five blocks away. And when we look at the video that we get and we put it into the case and we make wanted flyers, we do connect it from that person to the same person and then look at that person and see that they are a recidivist and that they’re driving retail theft. And then what we’ve done is we’ve leveraged the prosecutors, not just within Manhattan but across the five boroughs to not only aggregate these crimes which means it’s a– it would become a grand larceny instead of a petty larceny, but we’ve also had great success in our trespass affidavit program across the City of New York–
[interposing] Right.

Where that person is– if they get arrested for a petty theft or actually grand larceny, they’re served a trespass affidavit. If they go back into that location and commit another crime therein, they’re then charged with a burglary. And we’ve had over 90 percent arraignment rate on the burglary across the city working with the prosecutors and it really has substantially decreased the retail theft

across the city. I will also say, almost 50 percent of the retail theft complaints in New York City are solved with an arrest. That’s incredible.
Alright.
Prior to two years ago, it was about 33 percent, and now we’re closer to 50 percent.
Okay.
And I would just say, retail theft fell 14 percent citywide last year, so the 20 percent that he was talking about for this year is on top of a 14 percent–
[interposing] Okay.
Decline and that tracks to when that new plan went into effect.
Alright. And domestic violence, is that up, down, and how are we doing with it?
Domestic violence is up.
I know.
And we have just done– completed a massive reorganization of the Department to address it. Domestic violence isn’t just up this year. This has been really since–
[interposing] But it’s good in a sense people are reporting which is the other thing.

But it’s up meaningfully since I would say the pandemic, and we have just completed a massive reorganization of the Department so that we can better address not only the crime, but improve how we deal with victims. And so a lot of that reorganization has been about one, improving the quality and the focus on DV investigations; two, doing a better job of hunting down DV perps; and three, is making sure that if you are a victim of domestic violence, you are not getting outreach from multiple different officers all asking you the same information, that we streamline who talks to victims and about what.
And it’s making a difference, you think, in terms of numbers or how is it going to impact–
[interposing] I think–
[interposing] Or it’s too soon to know?

I think that it will make a difference. I think it already has made a difference

in terms of the way we treat victims. We are now taking a victim-centered approach to domestic violence. Whether to the extent that it will bring DV numbers down, I don’t know. What I can tell you is those cases will be investigated in a more streamlined and effective and victim-centered way.
Okay. Thank you. And then finally just paperwork. I know– I mean, can you help– we know that there’s still a lot. Is it changing? I know we’ve talked about this in the past. If you–
[interposing] So, there’s a lot of paperwork.
There is.
There is too much paperwork.
Yes.

I actually find like the paperwork issue in the past has gotten politicized. Like, this is not a political statement. There’s too much paperwork that the NYPD has to do, and I would love to work with this Council on streamlining it if the Council is open to it, both the paperwork and the general reporting requirements on this Department. Just requires a lot of resources to meet.

So, there’s reporting and then there’s if I have a broken window in my car– which I don’t have a car, but if I had one then I go to the precinct. Is that still a paper-mandated report or is that online?
Well, any crime– any crime com– when I say paperwork, I don’t mean crime–
[interposing] There’s two kinds. Yeah, there’s the reporting and then there’s the paperwork that we citizens have to fill out when we have a crime situation and that the officers have to fill out.
So, we have digitized a number of the forms that our officers have to fill out. The– over the past I don’t know, seven years, there are some that are still done on paper.

Okay. And can you get us a list of those? Or I’m not asking for more reporting. I do think that when you finish your tour, because we did go out with some tours, there’s still a lot of paperwork to be done. Can– and that perhaps could also be streamlined. And maybe we can help you do that. If there's too much reporting there.
I agree. I’m going to look forward to it. Thank you very much Council Member.
Thank you very much, Commissioner.

And thank you, Council Member Brewer. Next we’ll hear from Council Member Nurse and then from Majority Leader Shaun Breau. I also want to recognize that we’ve been joined by Council Member Justin Sanchez and Avilés.

Thank you, Chair. Good morning, Commissioner. I just have three questions. You’ve done some outreach recently about police communications technicians. It looks like their starting salary is from $42-$49,000 per year, and I think– it’s been communicated to me that very experienced folks are about $60,000 per year. Has there been any effort to bring that salary up?

So, unfortunately, the salaries for all of these positions are not really set by the agency. They are set through collective bargaining agreements that are largely led by the Office of Labor Relations. However, we have worked very closely with the union and Henry to do things to try to make the position more financially appealing

to applicants including how we administer this bonus that was put in a few years ago to make it so that more people are eligible for it, so it becomes a part of the general salary.

Yeah. And some of the concerns were because of the low salary, high turnover– and I understand you’re not directly in charge of it, but I’m putting it out here for the public. Low wages, high turnover, people are saying they’re frequently mandated to do 16-hour shifts very often.

Less than– too much, but less and less. So what was going on at 911 was that it basically wasn’t managed as far as I can tell. What I saw when I came in a year ago and looked at it was an unacceptably high number of call-taking delays, not because the police communications technicians weren’t doing their job, but because their managers weren’t allocating the staffing based on when calls come in. You know what time of day the most calls come in, and that's when our staffing was the lowest. And so there were a number of things that we were able to do working with the union on, you know,

12-hours, 10-hour tours, 8-hour tours, making sure we had the right number of squads working at the right time to not only improve our service to the public, but to I would say meaningfully bring down some of the forced overtime. But there still is quite a fair amount of it.

Fair enough. And then– just you had a lot in your testimony about international incidents. How many NYPD personnel are deployed outside the United States, and do you have a cost of that international–
[interposing] so, it's 12 countries, and the New York City Police Foundation picks up the cost associated with it, everything except, of course, the officer’s salary.
And what is that budget?
The–
